column1: #tags column:3
Define current and its unit; what does a negative current mean?
column2: i = dq/dt, in amperes (1 A = 1 C/s ≈ 6.24×10^18 elementary charges per second). Negative means the flow is opposite to the chosen reference arrow.

column1: Define voltage and its unit.
column2: Energy per unit charge between two points, v_AB = v_A − v_B = dw/dq, in volts (1 V = 1 J/C). Always between two points; a node voltage is relative to the reference node.

column1: State the three conditions of the lumped matter discipline.
column2: (1) No changing magnetic flux links any loop outside the elements; (2) no net charge accumulates inside an element (or node); (3) signals change slowly compared with the time waves take to cross the circuit.

column1: Which lumped condition gives KCL, and which gives KVL?
column2: Nodes store no charge (condition 2) plus charge conservation give KCL. No changing flux outside elements (condition 1) plus Faraday's law make ∮E·dl = 0, giving KVL.

column1: Passive sign convention: statement and consequence.
column2: Reference the current INTO the + terminal; then p = vi is the power ABSORBED. Negative p means the element delivers power.

column1: Why does SPICE report a negative current for a battery that is discharging?
column2: SPICE uses the passive convention for sources too: current is positive into the + terminal. A delivering source pushes current out of its + terminal, so it reads negative, and its @V[p] is negative.

column1: State Tellegen's theorem and why it holds.
column2: Σ v_k i_k = 0 over all branches (passive convention). Write v_k as node-voltage differences (KVL) and regroup by node; each node's currents sum to zero (KCL). No element laws used, so it holds for any lumped circuit.

column1: Lumped rule of thumb for digital edges, and the delay of FR-4 stripline?
column2: Lumped if one-way delay t_d < t_r/6. FR-4 stripline (εr ≈ 4.6): about 7.15 ps/mm, so 1 ns edges allow about 23 mm.

column1: Is mAh energy? Convert 225 mAh at 3.0 V.
column2: No: mAh is charge (1 mAh = 3.6 C). Energy = charge × voltage: 0.225 Ah × 3.0 V = 0.675 Wh = 2430 J.

column1: Average current of a duty-cycled device?
column2: I_avg = Σ D_k I_k (duty cycle × current for each activity, plus the always-on sleep current). Battery life = capacity / I_avg. A huge current at a tiny duty cycle can be a small share.

column1: Why is average power not V_avg × I_avg?
column2: P_avg is the average of v(t)·i(t); it depends on when v and i are large together. Only at DC (or with one factor constant) does it equal the product of averages.

column1: Distribution loss for power P at voltage V through resistance R?
column2: I = P/V, so loss = P²R/V² and loss fraction = PR/V². Doubling V quarters the loss; for equal loss the copper area can shrink by the square of the voltage ratio.

column1: Efficiency of a chain of converters?
column2: η_total = η_1 × η_2 × … ; loss = P_out(1/η − 1). Example: 97% × 90% = 87.3%, so 1 kW out needs 1145.5 W in.

column1: How much current does a 1 kW chip draw at 0.8 V, and what path resistance keeps the drop under 2%?
column2: 1250 A; 2% of 0.8 V = 16 mV, so R ≤ 16 mV / 1250 A = 12.8 µΩ. Hence regulators sit next to, under or inside the package.

column1: Ohm's law: forms, units and the sign condition.
column2: v = Ri, i = Gv, G = 1/R; ohm = V/A, siemens = A/V. Holds as written with the passive sign convention; with the current arrow out of the + terminal it is v = −Ri.

column1: Three forms of resistor power, and which resistor dissipates more in series and in parallel?
column2: p = vi = i²R = v²/R ≥ 0. In series (same i) the larger R dissipates more; in parallel (same v) the smaller R dissipates more.

column1: Sheet resistance and squares.
column2: R_□ = ρ/t (Ω per square); R = R_□ × L/W. A square of any size has R_□. 1 oz PCB copper (35 µm) ≈ 0.49 mΩ/□.

column1: Copper's resistivity and temperature coefficient (IACS).
column2: 1.7241 µΩ·cm at 20 °C (17.2 mΩ per meter per mm²); +0.393 %/°C. A 65 °C rise adds about 26%.

column1: Element laws of short, open, ideal voltage source, ideal current source.
column2: Short: v = 0 for any i. Open: i = 0 for any v. Voltage source: v = v_s for any i (0 V source = short). Current source: i = i_s for any v (0 A source = open).

column1: Which ideal-source connections are impossible?
column2: Unequal voltage sources in parallel; a shorted voltage source; unequal current sources in series; an open current source. They violate KVL or KCL; real sources (with internal resistance) turn them into large currents.

column1: Practical source model and its two named points.
column2: v = V_oc − R_int i. Open-circuit voltage V_oc (i = 0); short-circuit current I_sc = V_oc/R_int (v = 0). Equivalent: I_sc in parallel with R_int.

column1: Find R_int from two load measurements.
column2: R_int = (V1 − V2)/(I2 − I1), the slope of the terminal line; then V_oc = V1 + I1 R_int. E.g. 3.90 V open, 3.75 V at 0.375 A → 0.40 Ω.

column1: Two cells of 4.20 V and 3.60 V, 50 mΩ each, in parallel: what happens?
column2: 6.0 A circulates (0.60 V / 0.10 Ω); terminal 3.90 V; 3.6 W of heat; the weak cell is charged. Never parallel unmatched cells.

column1: E-series: what E12, E24, E96 mean and their steps.
column2: n values per decade spaced ≈ 10^(1/n): E12 ≈ ×1.21 (±10%), E24 ≈ ×1.10 (±5%), E96 ≈ ×1.024 (±1%). IEC 60063. Several E12/E24 values (2.7, 3.3, 3.9, 4.7, 8.2…) are historical, not pure geometric.

column1: Thick-film versus thin-film chip resistors.
column2: Thick film: ±1–5%, ±100–200 ppm/K, cheapest, most common. Thin film: ±0.1–1%, ±10–50 ppm/K, about 10× better on both, at a premium.

column1: Worst-case analysis of an LED resistor current.
column2: Take each tolerance to the limit that pushes the output furthest: I_max = (V_s,max − V_LED)/R_min, I_min = (V_s,min − V_LED)/R_max. Supply variation acts on the small difference V_s − V_LED, so it often dominates.

column1: Static versus incremental resistance of a diode at 1 mA.
column2: Static v/i ≈ 0.6548 V / 1 mA = 655 Ω; incremental dv/di = V_T/I ≈ 25.9 Ω. Small signals see the incremental value.

column1: Why do the lowest-value shunts have worse TCR?
column2: The element alloy is low-TCR (<20 ppm/°C), but copper terminations (~3900 ppm/°C) become a larger share of a sub-milliohm total (an inference; one family goes from ±35 to ±350 ppm/°C).

column1: How many independent KCL and KVL equations does a circuit with n nodes and b branches have?
column2: n − 1 KCL (the n-th is implied) and b − n + 1 KVL (one per link of a spanning tree; the meshes, for a planar circuit). Total b, to pair with b element laws.

column1: Series and parallel resistors: rules and two mental shortcuts.
column2: Series: R add, same current. Parallel: G add, same voltage; R1∥R2 = R1R2/(R1+R2). N equal in parallel = R/N; parallel result < smallest resistor.

column1: Voltage divider and current divider formulas (two resistors).
column2: Voltage: v2 = v R2/(R1 + R2). Current: i1 = i R2/(R1 + R2), the crossover: the smaller resistor takes the larger current.

column1: Loaded divider: output and error.
column2: v_out = v_in (R2∥RL)/(R1 + R2∥RL). Divider looks like a source of R1∥R2; error ≈ (R1∥R2)/RL: 10× load ≈ 9%, 100× ≈ 1%, 1000× ≈ 0.1%.

column1: Why is a divider's ratio error up to twice each resistor's tolerance?
column2: The output depends on R1/R2; the worst case moves them in opposite directions, so the ratio error approaches the sum of the tolerances (1%+1% → ~2%). Matched networks track and do far better.

column1: Wheatstone bridge output and balance.
column2: v_out = V[R2/(R1+R2) − R4/(R3+R4)]; balanced (0) when R1R4 = R2R3. At balance the excitation drops out.

column1: Quarter-, half- and full-bridge outputs for a small ΔR/R.
column2: Quarter ≈ (V/4)(ΔR/R), nonlinearity ≈ ΔR/(2R). Half (equal and opposite) = (V/2)(ΔR/R), linear. Full = V(ΔR/R), linear, with temperature cancellation.

column1: Strain gauge: gauge factor and the size of the signal.
column2: ΔR/R = GF·ε, GF ≈ 2 for foil. 1000 µε → 0.2%; a 2.5 V quarter bridge gives about 1.25 mV, so bridges feed instrumentation amplifiers.

column1: Delta-to-wye and wye-to-delta formulas.
column2: Δ→Y: R_a = R_ab R_ca / (R_ab + R_bc + R_ca) (the two touching a, over the sum). Y→Δ: R_ab = (R_aR_b + R_bR_c + R_cR_a)/R_c (over the opposite one). Equal: R_Y = R_Δ/3.

column1: R–2R ladder: why only two values?
column2: Looking onward from every node is 2R∥2R = R, so current halves at each rung: binary-weighted currents from R and 2R only; accuracy depends on the R:2R ratio, easy to match on a chip.
